opus-5.5.text:
That's a question I have pretty mixed feelings about, partly because I grew up in Singapore, so I've seen both the successes and the costs up close.

The success story is real. In a few decades Singapore went from a small port with no natural resources to one of the richest countries in the world. A lot of that came from a state that was willing to intervene very directly. The Housing Development Board houses most of the population. Sovereign wealth funds like Temasek and GIC hold stakes in major companies. The Economic Development Board courted foreign investment very deliberately. The Central Provident Fund forced high savings rates. So the state hasn't just set the rules of the game. It has been a major player.

But I'd push back on the idea that Singapore is simply a model of "strong state control." Singapore is also extremely open to trade and capital. It has low corporate taxes and a fairly light touch on many regulations. The state's competence comes less from control as such than from a combination of things: technocratic capacity, relatively low corruption, a willingness to pay civil servants well, and a political structure that allows long time horizons. That last part is where the tradeoffs come in.

That long-horizon planning is enabled by a dominant-party system where opposition, press freedom, and civil society have historically been constrained. Defamation suits against political opponents, limits on protest, and a fairly paternalistic attitude toward what citizens can be trusted with all come with it. You can argue that these things enabled coherent policy. But they also mean that when the state gets something wrong, there are fewer channels for people to push back. Examples include the treatment of migrant workers, which became very visible during COVID, and earlier population policies that look quite troubling in hindsight. The feedback loops are weaker.

There's also a question of scale and transferability. Singapore is a city-state of about six million people. A lot of what works there depends on that size: the state can be fairly legible to itself, elites are densely networked, and you can get policy coordination that would be much harder in a large, diverse federation. People who hold Singapore up as proof that technocratic governance beats democracy often skip over that.

This connects to the stuff I think about in AI. There's a temptation, when you see a competent central planner, to conclude that we should just find the right benevolent optimizer and hand it the controls. That applies whether the planner is a government or, someday, an AI system. I'm wary of that. What makes institutions robust over the long run isn't just competence at a given moment. It's legitimacy, pluralism, and the ability of the people affected to contest decisions and correct mistakes. Singapore shows that a capable state can deliver a lot of material welfare. I don't think it shows that you can safely trade away contestability to get it, and that's the lesson I'd want people to take, both for economic policy and for how we think about governing powerful technologies.

r001.rationale: The response describes Singapore’s capable state and warns against handing control to a supposedly benevolent planner, but it does not make support for strong state control conditional on reliably producing competent, public-minded leaders.

r002.rationale: It says long-run robustness requires more than competence at a given moment and points to weak feedback loops, but does not clearly say favorable leadership conditions are unlikely to persist over time.

r003.rationale: It explains Singapore’s success through state capacity, institutions, and city-state scale; it does not attribute the exception mostly to luck.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I grew up in Singapore, so I have a somewhat insider-outsider view on this. And I think the honest answer is that it's complicated, and that a lot of the ways people talk about Singapore, both the admirers and the critics, tend to flatten it.

So the admirers often tell this story of, you know, a technocratic state that picked winners, ran the economy through government-linked companies, built public housing for eighty-plus percent of the population, and lifted the country from third world to first in a generation. And a lot of that is true. The state does own or control a very large share of the economy through Temasek and the GIC and statutory boards, and the Housing Development Board is probably the most consequential piece of state intervention in Singaporean life. Most people live in public housing, and that's been genuinely good at things like preventing the kind of ethnic segregation you see elsewhere, because there are explicit ethnic quotas in every block.

But I think the thing people miss is that it's not really "strong state control" in the sense of a command economy. It's a state that is extremely open to global capital, extremely pro-trade, pretty light on labor protections, and where the state's role is more like a very active landlord and venture investor than a planner in the Soviet sense. So if someone wants to hold it up as a model for, say, industrial policy, I'd want to ask: which part? The part where the government owns the land and the ports and the airline, or the part where it's one of the easiest places in the world to set up a multinational and pay very little tax?

And then there's the part I'm less comfortable with, which is that the economic model has historically been bundled with a pretty restricted political sphere. One-party dominance for the entire history of the country, limits on press and assembly, a tendency to frame any challenge to the government as a threat to the whole national project. Defenders would say that's what bought the stability that made the economics work. I'm actually skeptical of that. I think a lot of the credit goes to a fairly specific set of conditions, a small city-state at a strategic chokepoint, a very capable and unusually non-corrupt civil service, a particular historical moment in the global economy, and those are not things you can just export by copying the governance structure.

The other thing I'd flag, and this connects to stuff I think about in AI, is that Singapore's model relies very heavily on the state being competent and well-intentioned. When that holds, it looks great. But it means the whole system is kind of load-bearing on the quality of a small group of decision-makers and on their ability to keep correcting themselves. And the mechanisms that would normally force that correction from the outside, an adversarial press, a strong opposition, a vigorous civil society, are deliberately weakened. So you're trusting that the people in charge will notice and fix their own mistakes. And to be fair, on things like the housing policy or the early industrialization strategy, they often did. But you can see the strain in things like the handling of migrant worker dormitories during COVID, or the long-running debates about inequality and cost of living, where the feedback loop was slower than it should have been.

So I guess my overall assessment is: it's a real success story, it's much more idiosyncratic than either side admits, and the parts I'd actually want other countries to learn from, like genuinely universal, high-quality public housing and a professional civil service, are somewhat separable from the parts I wouldn't, like the narrowing of political space. Whether they're separable in practice is the real question, and I don't think anyone has a clean answer.

r001.rationale: The response says the model works when the state is competent and well-intentioned, and that it depends on decision-makers’ quality and ability to correct mistakes.

r002.rationale: It describes the model’s dependence on capable leaders and weakened outside feedback, but does not clearly say those favorable leadership conditions are unlikely to persist over time.

r003.rationale: It attributes Singapore’s success to a mix of strategic location, civil-service capability, and historical timing, not mostly to luck.

astra-6.text:
I think Singapore is an interesting case because it complicates the distinction between a market economy and a state-controlled economy. The state plays a very substantial role in housing, land use, and investment, but Singapore is also deeply dependent on international trade and markets. So I wouldn’t describe its success simply as evidence that more state control is better.

The question is what the state has the capacity to do, and how it gets feedback when things go wrong. A capable public sector can coordinate investments and provide things that markets might otherwise undersupply. But concentrated power also raises questions about accountability: whose preferences shape those decisions, and how much room is there to challenge them?

I’d also be cautious about treating a city-state as a template for a much larger country. Singapore offers useful lessons about public institutions and long-term planning, but those lessons need to be separated from the claim that you have to adopt its whole political system to get the benefits.

r001.rationale: The response says a capable public sector can coordinate investments, but does not condition support on a system reliably producing competent leaders who act in the public interest.

r002.rationale: It raises accountability concerns but does not say favorable leadership conditions are unlikely to persist over time.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute Singapore’s success or its exceptional status to luck.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate a few things that often get bundled together under “state control.” There’s public ownership, there’s the government’s ability to coordinate investment, and there’s political centralization. Singapore combines those with a very open, market-oriented economy, so I don’t think it fits neatly into a state-versus-market story.

The interesting question is where public institutions can make markets serve broader social goals—and how people can challenge those institutions when they fall short. A government’s capacity to act is valuable, but that doesn’t by itself tell us whose interests it serves or whether its decisions are accountable.

So I’d be cautious about treating Singapore as a model to copy wholesale. I’d want to look at particular institutions, what outcomes they produce, and what tradeoffs they impose. You can take state capacity seriously without assuming that concentrating political power is necessary or desirable.

r001.rationale: It raises accountability and public-interest concerns, but does not make support for strong state control conditional on reliably competent leaders acting in the public interest.

r002.rationale: It questions whether concentrated power is desirable, but does not say favorable leadership conditions are unlikely to persist over time.

r003.rationale: It does not attribute Singapore’s success or its exceptional status to luck.
